claims.text: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 can be produced by conventional powder consolidation such as spark-plasma sintering.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops radiation-induced precipitates after irradiation to approximately 8 dpa at 600°C.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening under the stated irradiation conditions.
Adding 0.5–1 vol% Y2O3 nanoparticles before consolidation will reduce or prevent radiation-induced precipitation in W38Ta36Cr15V11 at approximately 8 dpa and 600°C.
Y2O3 nanoparticles introduced into the precursor powder will become uniformly distributed along grain boundaries and within grains during sintering.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as sinks for irradiation-generated vacancies and interstitials.
Point-defect absorption by Y2O3 nanoparticles will reduce the local defect supersaturation that drives radiation-induced precipitation.
The reduced point-defect supersaturation will impede solute clustering and precipitation.
Y2O3 nanoparticles located at grain boundaries will pin those boundaries.
Grain-boundary pinning by Y2O3 will improve microstructural stability during irradiation and high-temperature bulk processing.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have a lower precipitate density or extent of precipitation than the unmodified alloy after irradiation to approximately 8 dpa at 600°C.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain similarly negligible irradiation hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
Y2O3 addition will produce a microstructure more suitable for practical bulk fabrication.
The proposed benefits apply up to approximately 8 dpa and around 600°C.
Energetic-particle irradiation to approximately 8 dpa at 600°C is relevant to fusion applications.
